title: Ada's Rule
excerpt: The market returns to the crossroads on the first Friday of the month, and Ada has one rule about it.
content:
The market came to the crossroads the way weather comes — announced by the dogs, denied by the adults, and believed instantly by every child in town.

It set up on the first Friday of each month, between the broken streetlight and the borehole, and by sunset there were forty stalls under forty lanterns, selling things no warehouse had ever stocked: your grandfather's laugh, the smell of your mother's kitchen on a Tuesday, the exact weight of a promise you made when you were twelve.

Everyone lost things. The market sold them back.

Ada had a rule about the market, and the rule was simple: she did not trade there. Not once. Not ever. Not since the year she turned fourteen and made the mistake of buying back something she had lost, and learned what the market charges when the thing you're buying back is not a thing at all.

She walked past it every month with her eyes forward and her hands in her pockets, and she taught her little brother to do the same.

Which is why it was such a problem, this particular Friday, when the market set up early, and the first stall on the row — the one you always passed first, the one with the old woman who never aged and never forgot — was selling, in a small glass jar with a hand-written label:

Ada's voice. Sold by her sister.

## The Price of Getting It Back

Her sister was sixteen and clever and drowning, and everyone in town knew it, and no one in town said it. Ada had heard the argument through the wall the night before. She had heard what her sister was willing to give up to keep the family fed one more month.

She just hadn't known that the market was listening.

"It's a fair trade," said the old woman, uncorking the jar so Ada could hear — really hear — her own laugh from three years ago, before the arguing started, before the nights got long. "The market doesn't cheat. It only asks what the thing is worth to the person who lost it."

"And what does it think my voice is worth?"

The old woman smiled, and for the first time in forty years of first Fridays, she looked genuinely sorry.

"It thinks your voice is worth exactly what your sister paid for it," she said. "Come back at closing and ask me the question you actually came to ask."

Ada looked at the lanterns, all forty of them, guttering in a wind that wasn't blowing.

"And if I don't?"

"Then at dawn," the old woman said gently, "your sister forgets she ever had you at all — and the market keeps the change."
